sections.section_title: The Announcement of the Passover and the Plot
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the structural closing formula ('when Jesus had finished all these sayings') marking the end of the fifth discourse, Jesus's announcement that the Son of Man will be delivered up at Passover, and the chief priests and elders gathering at Caiaphas's palace to plot Jesus's arrest by stealth.

The neutral reading presents an unnamed woman anointing Jesus's head with costly ointment -- enacting the act that defines his identity as Christos (anointed one) -- which Jesus interprets as preparation for his burial, declaring that her act will be proclaimed wherever the gospel is preached.

The neutral reading presents Judas, identified emphatically as 'one of the twelve,' going to the chief priests to negotiate the betrayal of Jesus for thirty pieces of silver -- the contemptuous price of a slave from Zechariah 11:12-13 -- and from that moment seeking an opportune time to hand him over.
sections.relevance: The passage presents an insider at the highest level of proximity -- one of the twelve, personally called and commissioned by Jesus -- initiating the betrayal from within the circle. The neutral reading emphasizes the juxtaposition with the anointing: 'extravagant devotion followed by calculated treachery, both from people within the circle around Jesus.' The verb paradidomi (to hand over) is the same verb Jesus used of himself in verse 2, showing that the divine purpose and the human treachery converge on the same action. Judas's trajectory from the innermost circle to active betrayal demonstrates that proximity to Jesus and inclusion among his chosen twelve does not render standing irrevocable.
key_phrases: what will you give me if I deliver him over to you
from that moment he sought an opportunity to betray him

sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the disciples preparing the Passover as Jesus directed, with Jesus declaring 'my time is at hand' (ho kairos mou engys estin), using the word kairos for the decisive moment charged with significance.

The neutral reading presents Jesus at the Passover table identifying one of the twelve as the betrayer ('one of you will betray me'), pronouncing woe on the betrayer ('it would have been better for that man if he had not been born'), and noting that Judas addresses Jesus as 'Rabbi' while the other disciples address him as 'Lord.'
sections.relevance: The passage presents the most severe judgment in the document -- 'it would have been better for that man if he had not been born' -- pronounced against an insider who shared the covenantal meal. The neutral reading identifies the shared dish as an act of 'intimate fellowship' and notes that 'to betray one who shares your table is the most fundamental violation of covenant hospitality.' The Passover itself was a covenantal act, making 'betrayal at this table betrayal of the covenant community.' The passage holds divine purpose and human responsibility together without resolution: 'The Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man.' Scripture's fulfillment does not absolve the human instrument. An insider at the covenant meal faces catastrophic judgment for subsequent conduct.
key_phrases: one of you will betray me
woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed
it would have been better for that man if he had not been born

sections.section_title: The Reinterpretation of the Passover Meal
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents Jesus reinterpreting the Passover elements as 'my body' and 'my blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins,' combining the Sinai covenant ratification (Exodus 24:8), Jeremiah's new covenant promise (Jeremiah 31:31-34), and Isaiah's suffering servant (Isaiah 53:12), then declaring he will not drink wine again until he drinks it new 'with you in my Father's kingdom.'
sections.relevance: The passage establishes the new covenant in Jesus's blood as the basis for the forgiveness of sins -- the very forgiveness Jeremiah's new covenant promised. The neutral reading notes that Jesus 'locates the forgiveness of sins not in the temple's sacrificial system, not in John's baptism, but in his own poured-out blood.' The covenant blood is poured out 'for many' (peri pollon), drawing on Isaiah 53's 'multitude.' The promise of future communion 'with you in my Father's kingdom' implies that the relationship enacted at the table continues beyond death into the kingdom. If the new covenant secures forgiveness and the covenant bond endures into the kingdom, this bears on the permanence of standing: the covenant is established by divine initiative and sealed in Jesus's blood, not in human performance.
key_phrases: this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins
I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom

sections.section_title: The Prediction of Desertion and Peter's Protest
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents Jesus predicting that all the disciples will skandalizo ('fall away') that night, citing Zechariah 13:7 ('I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered'), then promising regathering after resurrection ('I will go before you to Galilee'), followed by Peter's emphatic protest and Jesus's prediction of Peter's threefold denial before the rooster crows.
sections.relevance: The passage presents the reality that ALL insiders -- including Peter who professed willingness to die -- will fall away under pressure. The verb skandalizo connects to the rocky-ground hearer who 'falls away' under tribulation (13:21) and the 'many' who will skandalizo during persecution (24:10). Peter's predicted denial activates the 10:33 warning: 'whoever denies me before others, I also will deny before my Father in heaven.' However, the regathering promise in v.32 ('after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee') shows that the shepherd's initiative restores the scattered flock, tempering the conditionality. The passage demonstrates that insiders can and do fail catastrophically, but also that the shepherd's commitment to regathering survives their failure.
key_phrases: you will all fall away because of me this night
I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered
after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee
before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times

sections.summary: The neutral reading presents Jesus in Gethsemane praying three times for the cup of divine wrath to pass, each time submitting to the Father's will ('your will be done' -- the exact language of the Lord's Prayer at 6:10), while the three disciples who witnessed the transfiguration sleep through his anguish despite being told to 'watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation.'

The neutral reading presents Judas ('one of the twelve' for the third time) betraying Jesus with a kiss, Jesus's refusal of violent resistance ('all who take the sword will perish by the sword') and his declaration that he could summon twelve legions of angels but refrains so that the Scriptures may be fulfilled, culminating in the fulfillment of 26:31: 'all the disciples left him and fled.'

sections.section_title: The Trial Before the High Priest
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the Sanhedrin seeking false testimony, Jesus's silence fulfilling Isaiah 53:7, and his declaration before the high priest combining Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13 -- 'from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven' -- which the high priest declares blasphemy, leading to the death sentence and physical abuse.

The neutral reading presents Peter's threefold denial of Jesus in the courtyard of the high priest, escalating from simple denial to sworn denial to denial under self-invoked curse (katathematizo), using the distancing phrase 'I do not know the man' three times, followed by the rooster's crow and Peter's bitter weeping.
sections.relevance: The passage presents the foremost disciple -- the one who confessed Jesus as Christ (16:16), who was given the keys of the kingdom (16:19), who declared he would die before denying (26:35) -- denying Jesus three times before a servant girl, bystanders, and guards. The neutral reading explicitly connects the denial to 10:33: 'The verb arneomai (to deny) is the specific word Jesus predicted, and 10:33 states: whoever denies me before others, I also will deny before my Father in heaven.' Peter's progressive violations of Jesus's own teaching (swearing oaths contrary to 5:33-37, invoking curses) show an insider spiraling deeper into failure. The passage demonstrates that even the most prominent insider can fall catastrophically under pressure, activating the very warning Jesus gave about the consequences of denial.
key_phrases: I do not know the man
he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear
he went out and wept bitterly
